findings.description: AWS access key and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is visible via the instance metadata service and Terraform state to anyone with read access, allowing credential theft.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, meaning data at rest on the volume is stored unencrypted and vulnerable to exposure if the underlying storage is compromised or snapshots are shared.

The snapshot is created from an unencrypted volume and does not enforce encryption itself, so the snapshot data remains unencrypted at rest and encryption cannot be added afterward without re-creation.
Ingress rule allows TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the instance's management port to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.

Ingress rule allows TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no compensating controls (e.g., WAF, TLS termination), exposing the web service to unrestricted internet traffic and defeating network segmentation.
Egress rule allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, providing no network-level constraint on outbound traffic and increasing risk of data exfiltration if the instance is compromised.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive public IP addresses, increasing exposure to the internet.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive public IP addresses, increasing exposure to the internet.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (e.g., aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic logs stored unencrypted.

The bucket has no associated public access block or bucket policy restricting access, and force_destroy is enabled, leaving it potentially accessible/exposed with no explicit safeguard against public exposure.
